canonicalExplanation.summary: A **scalar** holds one value: integers (`char`, `short`, `int`, `long`, `long long`, signed or `unsigned`), floating point (`float`, `double`), `bool` (from `<stdbool.h>`), enumerations and pointers. C sets only **minimum ranges**: `int` is at least 16 bits (usually 32), `long` at least 32 (64 on Linux, 32 on Windows). Whether plain `char` is signed is up to the implementation. So **pick types by meaning**: `size_t` for sizes and counts of objects, `int32_t` from `<stdint.h>` when you need an exact width, `double` for measurements, `bool` for flags. Check real sizes with `sizeof`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner stores the number of items in an array as `unsigned int`. It works on their laptop, but a code reviewer points out that on large 64-bit data sets the count can exceed what unsigned int holds. An object count uses size_t because it represents object sizes and array bounds rather than assuming unsigned int has the same range. In this lesson you'll choose and declare a suitable scalar type while avoiding unjustified size assumptions.

examples.title: Counting items with size_t
examples.situation: An object count uses size_t because it represents object sizes and array bounds rather than assuming unsigned int has the same range.
walkthrough: **An object count uses size_t:** `size_t count = sizeof marks / sizeof marks[0];`.
**It represents object sizes and array bounds:** sizeof itself returns size_t, so no conversion is needed.
**Rather than assuming unsigned int has the same range:** on 64-bit systems size_t is usually 64 bits; the loop index will also be size_t.
examples.result: The count is correct for any array the system can hold.

examples.title: The signed char surprise
examples.situation: A learner reads bytes into a plain char and checks `if (c > 127)` to detect high bytes. It never triggers on their machine.
walkthrough: Plain char is signed there, so byte 200 reads as -56.
Use unsigned char (or uint8_t) for raw bytes.
examples.result: High bytes are detected on every platform.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: C guarantees int is exactly 32 bits and plain char is always signed on every supported system.
misconceptions.correction: C only guarantees minimum ranges, and char signedness varies between implementations. Use fixed-width types when width matters and check with sizeof.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The signed char surprise", why did 200 read as -56?

analogy.example: Choosing a type is like **choosing a container**: a measuring jug for liquid (double), an egg box for countable items (size_t), a single light switch for yes/no (bool). C tells you the **minimum** size of each container, not the exact one, so you check the label (sizeof).
limitations: Containers overflow visibly; integers overflow silently.
Exact-size boxes exist when you need them (int32_t).

farTransfer.prompt: Write a program that prints sizeof for char, short, int, long, long long, float, double, size_t and a pointer. Run it (or compare published tables) for 64-bit Linux and 64-bit Windows and explain the differences.

remediation.explanation: For each variable ask: **what does it mean (count, measurement, flag, byte, exact field)?** Then pick the type that matches that meaning, not your machine's habits.

recap.summary: To choose scalar types well, pick by meaning (size_t for sizes and counts, fixed-width integers when width matters, double for measurements, bool for flags, unsigned char for bytes), remember C only guarantees minimum ranges and leaves char signedness to the implementation, and check with sizeof.
